enrichment.short_title: Income support deprivation of capital where car purchased to repay friend's loan

statutes_considered.title: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

key_facts: Mrs Jones received £57,000 from selling part of her garden in October 1999, exceeding the £8,000 capital limit for income support.
Most proceeds were used to pay pressing mortgage arrears, credit card debts and other creditors; those repayments were accepted as proper capital reductions.
On 1 December 1999 she used £13,250 to buy a BMW under an arrangement with friend and creditor Mr Smith, who had a £17,000 loan repayable on demand and had sought repayment or security.
The tribunal treated the car purchase as deprivation of capital for the purpose of securing income support; the Commissioner upheld that decision.
The Court of Appeal held there was no evidence the transaction was for the prohibited purpose where an immediately repayable debt was being satisfied.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with leave from a Social Security Commissioner's decision dismissing Mrs Jones's appeal against an appeal tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claimant entitled to income support from 13 October 1999 onwards; respondent ordered to pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant repays an immediately repayable debt, a tribunal must decide as a question of fact whether the disposal was for the purpose of securing entitlement to income support; repayment of a debt genuinely demanded is cogent evidence against that purpose, and a creditor's lack of pressure after security is taken does not answer whether the payment at the time of purchase was a prohibited deprivation of capital.
legal_issues: Whether purchase of a car to repay an on-demand loan was deprivation of capital under regulation 51(1)
Whether the car was a disregarded personal possession under Schedule 10 paragraph 10
Whether an incumbrance in favour of the creditor should be deducted under regulation 49(a)(ii)
Whether immediately repayable debts not yet demanded must always be treated as retained capital

notes: Leading judgment on equitable set-off against assignee landlord; full reasoning available.

enrichment.short_title: Equitable set-off of prior landlord's disrepair damages against assigned rent arrears
key_facts: Mr Smith, a statutory tenant in Beckenham, withheld rent from December 1995 after prolonged disrepair works under the previous landlord Mr Walker.
Mr Muscat bought the freehold in October 1999 inheriting £3,860.13 rent arrears and later served notice to quit and brought possession proceedings.
The county court judge held Muscat liable for £2,000 disrepair since October 1999 but held no set-off was available for Walker's earlier breaches.
The tenant accepted that if arrears stood at £3,232.06 an outright possession order was unappealable.
The Court of Appeal held a tenant may set off unliquidated damages for a predecessor landlord's repairing breach against rent arrears assigned to a new landlord.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Tenant's appeal with leave from Bromley County Court possession and rent arrears proceedings, assigned directly to the Court of Appeal under CPR 52.14.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; claim and counterclaim remitted to the county court for trial on quantum and possession.
enrichment.ratio: A tenant sued by an assignee landlord for assigned rent arrears may rely on equitable set-off for unliquidated damages for the assignor's breach of repairing covenant, because an assignee of a chose in action takes subject to equities available against the assignor; general equitable set-off cannot be asserted against a third party who is not the claimant, but assignment rules govern this landlord and tenant case.
legal_issues: Whether equitable set-off is available for a previous lessor's disrepair against assigned rent arrears
Whether sections 141 and 142 of the Law of Property Act 1925 exclude equitable set-off on assignment of the reversion
Whether delay and availability of a direct claim against the previous landlord barred set-off

enrichment.short_title: Whether section 24(2) criteria apply when extending appointment of leasehold manager
key_facts: A manager had been appointed for Orchard Court under section 24 of the 1987 Act because of disrepair and poor management.
Residents applied under section 24(9) to extend the manager's appointment for two years; the landlord opposed but did not pursue discharge.
The Leasehold Valuation Tribunal extended the appointment, finding it just and equitable; the Lands Tribunal refused leave to appeal.
The landlord argued section 24(2) thresholds must be re-satisfied whenever an order is varied, including extension of a manager's term.
Keene LJ held section 24(9) does not incorporate section 24(2) criteria for tenant applications and refused permission to appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal against the Lands Tribunal's refusal of leave to appeal from a Leasehold Valuation Tribunal decision.
enrichment.ratio: Section 24(9) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1987 draws a deliberate distinction from section 24(2): varying or extending an existing manager's appointment does not require the tribunal to be satisfied afresh of the section 24(2) grounds, though it must have regard to relevant considerations and, for landlord applications, section 24(9A) applies separately.
legal_issues: Whether section 24(2) criteria must be met to extend a manager's appointment under section 24(9)
Whether use of 'just and equitable' rather than 'just and convenient' invalidated the tribunal's decision
Whether the Court of Appeal had jurisdiction to hear an appeal from a refusal of leave by the Lands Tribunal

enrichment.short_title: Planning call-in challenge where Inspector did not respond to abuse-of-power submission
key_facts: Cherwell District Council resolved to grant planning permission for a hotel, golf clubhouse, driving range and community centre at Banbury Golf Centre.
Oxfordshire County Council requested call-in; the Secretary of State called in the application because of the nature, scale and location of development in open countryside.
After inquiry the Inspector and Secretary of State refused permission, finding conflict with local plan policy T5, PPG6, PPG7 and PPG13.

The claimant argued the Inspector and Secretary of State failed to respond to an Initial Legal Submission alleging the County Council's call-in request was an abuse of power and that its evidence deserved less weight.
Sullivan J held those preliminary matters were not material planning considerations or deserved no weight; refusal stood on planning merits.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to quash the Secretary of State's called-in planning decision.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; claimant ordered to pay agreed costs of £4,695.
enrichment.ratio: A Secretary of State's call-in decision is exercised independently for proper planning reasons; a local authority's motive in requesting call-in and arguments that call-in should not have occurred are not material planning considerations, and failure expressly to respond to such submissions does not render the decision unlawful where the principal planning issues were fully reasoned and could only have one outcome.
legal_issues: Whether failure to respond to the claimant's Initial Legal Submission breached the duty to give reasons
Whether alleged abuse of power by the county council in requesting call-in was a material planning consideration
Whether the quality of the county council's evidence on policy T5 was a material consideration requiring specific response

enrichment.short_title: London arbitration award enforced after late challenge and conflicting Chinese judgment
key_facts: Owners of the Joanna V issued bills of lading with a London arbitration clause after grounding at San Lorenzo and declaring general average.
Receivers and PICC provided salvage security, arrested the vessel in China and pursued salvage contribution proceedings in the Ningbo Maritime Court.
Donald Davies QC made a London arbitration award holding the receivers liable for general average and detention; receivers did not challenge jurisdiction within 28 days.
Chinese courts later held owners liable for salvage costs on merits, treating the dispute as not arising under the bills of lading.
Thomas J refused extension of time to challenge the award, granted leave to enforce it, and gave summary judgment striking out recognition of the Chinese judgment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial court applications concerning enforcement of a London maritime arbitration award, extension of time under the Arbitration Act 1996, and competing proceedings to recognise a Chinese maritime court judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Application to extend time refused; leave granted to enforce Davies award; summary judgment for owners against PICC and receivers' recognition claim.
enrichment.ratio: Where an arbitral tribunal rules on its own jurisdiction in a merits award, a party must challenge under section 67 within 28 days or lose that right under section 73; extension of time under section 80(5) should be refused where delay was deliberate and the owners suffered irremediable prejudice, and an earlier valid arbitration award giving rise to issue estoppel takes precedence over a later foreign judgment between privies.
legal_issues: Whether receivers lost the right to challenge arbitrator jurisdiction by failing to apply within 28 days
Whether time to challenge should be extended under section 80(5) of the Arbitration Act 1996
Whether owners submitted to Chinese court jurisdiction
Whether the London award or later Chinese judgment should be recognised and whether issue estoppel applied

enrichment.short_title: Tracing and sham-trust claims after Russo fraud on Shalson and Mimran investors
key_facts: Onofrio Russo induced Peter Shalson and related companies to part with £19.45m and defrauded Jean-Claude Mimran through Westbond International Bank and related structures.
Summary judgment of £20m was entered against Russo and £19.45m against WIB; Russo was committed for contempt and WIB was wound up.
Mimran parties sought to trace US$7.5m paid into Westland through WIB/PKB into the yacht Mosaique, Edenton loans and related assets.
Shalson took security over Edenton loans and structured Mosaique ownership through Cardinal and Braemar; Mimran's tracing into the Mosaique and Edenton loans failed.
Claims that the Brookscastle settlement was a sham against Cantrust failed; Cantrust parties settled during trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Multi-party Chancery trial following freezing orders, committal and summary judgment in fraud proceedings started March 2001, including Part 20 claims by Mimran parties.
enrichment.outcome: Mimran tracing and section 423 claims dismissed; claim against Cantrust dismissed; Mimran entitled to money judgments against Russo and WIB for US$8.5m, US$2.5m and US$7.5m plus interest; Oceanwave's claim against WIB failed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a trust settlement is executed by a trustee with honest intention to create a valid trust, it cannot be treated as a sham without proving the trustee was a knowing party to a pretence; granting security to a creditor for existing indebtedness is not a transaction at an undervalue under section 423; tracing fails where mixed funds passed through an overdrawn bank account and a bona fide purchaser for value without notice takes charged assets free of the trace.
legal_issues: Whether Mimran could trace payments through WIB and PKB into the Mosaique and Edenton loan assets
Whether the Brookscastle settlement was a sham enabling Russo to hide assets from creditors
Whether Cantrust dishonestly assisted Russo's breaches of trust
Whether charges granted to Shalson over Edenton loans were voidable under section 423

notes: Complete High Court directions judgment on police confidentiality in care proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: Disclosure of confidential police intelligence in care proceedings
key_facts: A local authority brought care proceedings in relation to several children of a mother with a history of drug addiction.
Police told social workers a black man believed to be a heroin and crack supplier was living at the mother's address but forbade disclosure because of a covert operation and informant risk.
Social workers visiting the home saw a man matching the description; children were nonetheless returned to the mother under interim care orders and a written agreement restricting overnight guests.
The local authority sought directions on whether and how to disclose the police information to the mother and other parties.

Wall J ordered disclosure of the substance of the allegation to the mother and wider documents to her solicitors subject to an Official Solicitor v K undertaking not to pass protected material to the client without further order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court directions application transferred from the county court in ongoing care proceedings, heard without notice to the mother initially.
enrichment.outcome: Mother to be told police information that a male believed to be a drug supplier was living at her address; solicitors may see wider court documents on undertaking; further disclosure to other parties reserved to circuit judge.
enrichment.ratio: In care proceedings the local authority must prove threshold facts on the balance of probabilities; non-disclosure of relevant information is exceptional, but police intelligence may be redacted so the lay parent receives the substance of the allegation while material identifying informants or compromising investigations is withheld from the client but may be shown to solicitors under court-controlled undertakings.
legal_issues: Whether police confidentiality prevented disclosure of drug-supplier intelligence to the mother
Whether Article 6 required the mother to be given notice and opportunity to answer the allegation
What form of redacted disclosure balanced child protection, fair trial and police operational security

enrichment.short_title: Criminal standard of proof for school exclusion where pupil accused of theft
key_facts: Schoolboy S was excluded for ten days after being found to have stolen a guitar from school.
Maurice Kay J dismissed judicial review, holding the standard was balance of probabilities with a seriousness gloss.
Respondents conceded after R (McCann) v Manchester Crown Court that the criminal standard applied to conduct amounting to a crime.
The Court of Appeal was not satisfied the decision-makers had applied the criminal standard on the contemporary material.
Permission to amend to challenge section 64's compatibility with Article 6 was refused because the case was moot.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Administrative Court judicial review of a governing body's decision upholding fixed-period exclusion.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed by concession; governing body decision quashed; school record to be amended; respondents ordered to pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where a school disciplinary accusation amounts to a crime under the general law, the head teacher and governors must be sure the pupil committed the act before finding it proved; McCann's criminal standard applies even outside criminal proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether balance of probabilities or criminal standard applies to theft allegations in school exclusions
Whether the governing body in fact applied the correct standard
Whether section 64 of the School Standards and Framework Act 1998 is incompatible with Article 6

notes: Complete personal injury appeal on earnings loss methodology.

enrichment.short_title: Future loss of earnings reduced where Smith v Manchester award was appropriate
key_facts: Claimant Hesp, a blacksmith and boat builder, suffered head and other injuries in a head-on collision caused by defendant Willemse driving on the wrong side of the road.
Leveson J awarded £212,620 including £53,000 past and £110,000 future loss of earnings.
Before the accident the claimant spent about four years building a valuable yacht rather than earning regularly; pre-accident accounts showed low profits.
The judge found modest brain damage with a serious psychological reaction reducing higher-level earning capacity.
The Court of Appeal upheld past loss assessment but substituted a £50,000 lump sum for future loss instead of a multiplier/multiplicand figure.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendant's appeal to the Court of Appeal against High Court assessment of special and general damages.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; future loss of earnings reduced from £110,000 to £50,000; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant's irregular pre-accident lifestyle and uncertain future career path make precise multiplier/multiplicand assessment unreliable, future loss of earnings should be assessed as a broad lump sum reflecting reduced earning capacity and disadvantage in the labour market rather than a fixed annual multiplicand.
legal_issues: Whether past loss of earnings was proved despite low formal accounts during boat-building project
Whether the judge's findings on brain injury and credibility supported the awards
Whether future loss should use multiplier/multiplicand or a Smith v Manchester lump sum

notes: Complete judgment on section 65(2) suitability and legitimate expectation history.

enrichment.short_title: Whether temporary maisonette discharged section 65(2) homelessness duty to disabled household
key_facts: Mrs Bibi applied as homeless in March 1991; Newham accepted a section 65(2) duty in May 1991 but believed it required eventual secure accommodation.
From October 1995 she occupied 34 Jade Close, a two-storey maisonette with internal stairs, under an assured shorthold tenancy arranged by the council.
Her disabled daughter's assessments indicated difficulty with stairs but the family occupied the property happily for about five years and told the council it was suitable.
After Awua, the authority retrospectively said Jade Close discharged the section 65(2) duty; earlier litigation established a legitimate expectation of secure housing but not automatic priority.
Owen J held Jade Close was suitable accommodation and refused a declaration that the section 65(2) duty still subsisted.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review seeking declaration that section 65(2) Housing Act 1985 duty remained owed; remaining live issue after earlier Bibi litigation and Court of Appeal decision on legitimate expectation.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; declaration refused; split costs order with no order before 21 February 2002 and claimant to pay authority's costs thereafter subject to detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Suitability under sections 65(2) and 69 of the Housing Act 1985 is a balancing exercise for a reasonable housing authority; internal stairs for a disabled household member are relevant but not conclusively determinative, and where the applicant consistently treated accommodation as satisfactory and lived there for years without complaint, a court should not hold it unsuitable simply because earlier welfare forms marked stairs as essential.
legal_issues: Whether 34 Jade Close was suitable accommodation discharging the section 65(2) duty
Whether the authority's internal medical assessment forms created mandatory suitability criteria
What practical effect remained from the legitimate expectation declared in earlier Bibi litigation
